name: Ramen
description: Ramen is a Japanese noodle soup built around wheat noodles and a seasoned broth, commonly flavored with soy sauce, miso, or salt. Bowls often include sliced pork, green onion, bamboo shoots, and a soft egg. It is eaten casually nationwide, with regional broths and specialized shops offering considerable variation.

name: Sushi
description: Sushi is a Japanese dish of vinegared rice paired with seafood, vegetables, or egg, served as hand-shaped pieces, rolls, or other forms. Fish may be raw, cooked, or preserved, and accompaniments include soy sauce, wasabi, and pickled ginger. It ranges from everyday conveyor-belt meals to formal dining.

name: Okonomiyaki
description: Okonomiyaki is a savoury griddle cake made from batter and shredded cabbage, with additions such as pork, seafood, or cheese. It is cooked on a hot plate and finished with sweet sauce, mayonnaise, seaweed, and bonito flakes. Osaka and Hiroshima styles differ in how ingredients and noodles are layered.

name: Onigiri
description: Onigiri is a portable Japanese rice snack shaped by hand into triangles, rounds, or other forms. Fillings commonly include salted salmon, pickled plum, tuna mayonnaise, or kelp, and nori may be wrapped around the outside. It is a familiar choice for school lunches, picnics, travel, and convenience-store meals.

name: Takoyaki
description: Takoyaki is a round street-food snack made by cooking a wheat-flour batter with pieces of octopus, pickled ginger, and green onion in a special molded pan. The hot balls are usually topped with sauce, mayonnaise, seaweed, and bonito flakes. Vendors often serve them at festivals, shopping streets, and casual gatherings.

name: Matcha parfait
description: Matcha parfait is a layered Japanese dessert combining green-tea ice cream or cream with ingredients such as sweet red beans, fruit, sponge cake, jelly, and mochi. Tall glasses show the contrasting textures, while syrup or whipped cream adds sweetness. It is especially common in tea cafés and dessert shops.

name: Soba
description: Soba is a Japanese noodle made primarily from buckwheat flour, giving it a lightly nutty flavor and firm texture. It may be served chilled with a dipping sauce or hot in a broth with toppings such as tempura or green onion. Slurping is ordinary, and soba is enjoyed year-round, including New Year's Eve.

name: Udon
description: Udon is a thick, chewy Japanese wheat noodle served hot in broth or chilled with a dipping sauce. Common toppings include green onion, fried tofu, tempura, meat, and a raw or cooked egg. It is a practical everyday meal, with broth seasonings and popular preparations varying between eastern and western Japan.

name: Tsukemen
description: Tsukemen is a ramen-style meal in which thick noodles are served separately from a concentrated dipping broth. Diners pick up noodles and dip them into the hot, strongly seasoned soup, often containing pork, seafood, or vegetables. The noodles may be requested hot or cold, and extra broth can be added afterward.

name: Hiyashi chuka
description: Hiyashi chuka is a chilled summer noodle dish made with wheat noodles topped by strips of egg omelette, cucumber, ham, chicken, or seafood. A tangy soy-vinegar or sesame dressing is poured over the arrangement before eating. It is commonly served at home and in casual restaurants during Japan's warm months.

name: Tempura
description: Tempura is a Japanese preparation of seafood or vegetables coated in a thin batter and fried briefly in hot oil, producing a crisp surface without a heavy crust. Shrimp, white fish, eggplant, pumpkin, and mushrooms are common choices. Pieces are served with dipping sauce and grated daikon, either as a meal or alongside noodles.

name: Tonkatsu
description: Tonkatsu is a thick pork cutlet coated in flour, egg, and coarse breadcrumbs before being deep-fried. It is sliced and served with shredded cabbage, mustard, rice, miso soup, and a sweet-tangy sauce. The dish is common in casual restaurants and also appears in sandwiches and curry meals.

name: Karaage
description: Karaage is a Japanese fried chicken preparation, usually made from bite-sized pieces marinated with soy sauce, ginger, garlic, and sake before being coated in starch. The pieces are fried until crisp and juicy, then served with lemon or mayonnaise. It is popular in home cooking, lunch boxes, pubs, and convenience stores.

name: Yakitori
description: Yakitori is a Japanese dish of chicken cut into small pieces, threaded onto skewers, and grilled over charcoal. Skewers may use thigh, breast, skin, liver, cartilage, or meatballs, and are seasoned with salt or a sweet soy-based tare. It is a classic casual food at izakaya, festivals, and neighborhood grill stalls.

name: Chicken nanban
description: Chicken nanban is a fried chicken dish coated or dressed with a sweetened vinegar sauce and topped with tartar sauce. The chicken is often served with shredded cabbage and rice, making a substantial meal. It developed in Miyazaki and is now found in family restaurants, lunch boxes, and home cooking across Japan.

name: Kushikatsu
description: Kushikatsu is a Japanese dish of meat, seafood, or vegetables threaded onto skewers, coated in batter and breadcrumbs, and deep-fried. Osaka's Shinsekai district is especially associated with the style, where skewers are dipped into shared sauce. The traditional etiquette is not to dip a partially eaten skewer twice.

name: Sukiyaki
description: Sukiyaki is a tabletop hot pot of thinly sliced beef, tofu, leafy vegetables, mushrooms, and noodles simmered in a sweet soy-based sauce. Ingredients are cooked gradually in a shallow pot and often dipped into beaten raw egg before eating. It is a popular winter meal for family gatherings and celebrations.

name: Shabu-shabu
description: Shabu-shabu is a hot-pot meal in which diners swish thin slices of meat through a simmering broth until cooked. Vegetables, tofu, and noodles are added to the same pot, then ingredients are dipped into ponzu or sesame sauce. The interactive cooking style suits relaxed group meals, especially in cooler weather.

name: Grilled gyūtan
description: Grilled gyūtan is a dish of thinly sliced beef tongue seasoned simply, often with salt, and cooked over a hot grill until browned and pleasantly firm. It is strongly associated with Sendai, where restaurants commonly serve it with barley rice, oxtail soup, and pickled vegetables. The texture distinguishes it from ordinary beef cuts.

name: Motsunabe
description: Motsunabe is a Fukuoka-style hot pot featuring beef or pork offal simmered with cabbage, garlic chives, tofu, and sometimes chili. The broth may be based on soy sauce, miso, or salt, and noodles are added near the end to absorb it. It is a sociable izakaya dish, especially popular in winter.

name: Katsudon
description: Katsudon is a rice bowl topped with sliced breaded pork cutlet gently simmered with onion and egg in a sweet soy-based broth. The crisp coating softens as it absorbs the sauce, while steamed rice makes the dish filling. It is a familiar diner and lunch choice, often associated with comforting everyday food.

name: Gyūdon
description: Gyūdon is a Japanese rice bowl topped with thinly sliced beef and onions simmered in dashi, soy sauce, and a mildly sweet seasoning. Pickled ginger, raw egg, or green onion may be added at the table. Fast-food gyūdon chains make it a convenient, affordable meal at almost any hour.

name: Oyakodon
description: Oyakodon is a Japanese rice bowl in which chicken and onion are simmered in a lightly sweet dashi-soy broth, then covered with softly set egg. The name reflects the use of chicken and egg together. It is a simple home-style meal, also widely served in casual restaurants and lunch counters.

name: Tendon
description: Tendon is a Japanese rice bowl topped with assorted tempura, commonly shrimp and vegetables, finished with a sweet soy-based tare. The sauce soaks into the steamed rice while the fried pieces retain some crispness. It is served in tempura restaurants and casual shops, often with miso soup and pickles.

name: Kaisendon
description: Kaisendon is a bowl of rice topped with an assortment of raw seafood, such as tuna, salmon, squid, scallops, and sea urchin. The rice may be plain or vinegared, and soy sauce with wasabi is used at the table. It is especially common in seafood markets and coastal towns.

name: Omurice
description: Omurice is a Japanese Western-style dish of seasoned chicken rice covered or wrapped in a soft omelette. Ketchup commonly flavors the rice and decorates the egg, though demi-glace and other sauces are also used. It appears in family restaurants, cafés, and home cooking, where the omelette style can range from firm to runny.

name: Ochazuke
description: Ochazuke is a simple Japanese dish of cooked rice covered with green tea, dashi, or another light broth. Toppings may include grilled salmon, pickled plum, salted fish, seaweed, or sesame. It is often eaten as a quick home meal, a late-night dish, or a gentle finish to an izakaya meal.

name: Takikomi gohan
description: Takikomi gohan is a Japanese rice dish cooked together with ingredients such as mushrooms, carrots, bamboo shoots, chicken, or seafood in dashi and soy-based seasoning. Because everything cooks in one pot, the grains absorb the savory flavors. It is common in home cooking and is often prepared with seasonal produce or served at gatherings.

name: Japanese curry rice
description: Japanese curry rice is a thick, mildly spiced stew served over short-grain rice. Onions, carrots, and potatoes are common, with chicken, pork, beef, or vegetables providing the main substance. Commercial curry roux makes it easy to prepare at home, and the dish is also a standard school-lunch and cafeteria meal.

name: Katsu curry
description: Katsu curry is a Japanese curry-rice dish topped with a sliced breaded pork cutlet, usually accompanied by shredded cabbage or pickles. The mild, thick curry contrasts with the crisp coating and turns a familiar cutlet into a hearty one-plate meal. It is common in casual curry shops, diners, and train-station restaurants.

name: Curry pan
description: Curry pan is a Japanese bread snack filled with thick curry and finished with a crisp fried or baked coating. The bread is shaped like a small bun so the filling can be eaten by hand, making it convenient for bakeries, school breaks, and train travel. Fillings may include meat or vegetables.

name: Gyoza
description: Gyoza is a Japanese dumpling usually filled with minced pork, cabbage, garlic chives, ginger, and garlic inside a thin wrapper. Most are pan-fried so one side becomes crisp, then steamed briefly and served with dipping sauce. They are common at ramen shops, izakaya, family tables, and frozen-food counters.

name: Chahan
description: Chahan is a Japanese-style fried rice dish stir-fried with cooked rice, egg, green onion, and ingredients such as pork, shrimp, or vegetables. Soy sauce, salt, and other seasonings provide a savory finish, while high heat keeps the grains separate. It is a practical restaurant and home dish for using leftover rice.

name: Nikuman
description: Nikuman is a soft wheat-flour bun steamed around a filling of seasoned minced pork, onion, and other aromatics. The warm, portable buns are sold at convenience stores, bakeries, and winter events, often as a quick snack. Similar steamed buns may contain sweet bean paste, curry, or other fillings.

name: Shumai
description: Shumai is a small steamed dumpling with a thin wrapper gathered around a filling, usually minced pork with onion and seasonings, or shrimp. The top remains open and may be marked with vegetables or roe. In Japan, shumai is eaten at Chinese-style restaurants, dim sum meals, bento shops, and train stations.

name: Edamame
description: Edamame is a Japanese snack of young soybeans cooked in their green pods, usually by boiling or steaming and seasoning with salt. The beans are squeezed directly from the pod rather than eaten with it. They are a familiar accompaniment to beer at izakaya, but also appear in home meals, salads, and frozen-food sections.

name: Agedashi tofu
description: Agedashi tofu is a Japanese tofu dish lightly coated and fried until the outside is crisp, then served in a warm dashi-based sauce. Grated daikon, green onion, ginger, and bonito flakes are common toppings. The contrast between the delicate fried surface and soft interior makes it a standard small dish at izakaya and Japanese restaurants.

name: Nikujaga
description: Nikujaga is a home-style Japanese stew of meat, potatoes, onions, and sometimes carrots or shirataki noodles simmered in dashi, soy sauce, sake, and sugar. Beef is common in western Japan and pork in eastern regions, though households vary. It is valued as an everyday family dish rather than restaurant food.

name: Taiyaki
description: Taiyaki is a fish-shaped cake made from pancake-like batter and cooked in a hinged mold. Sweet red bean paste is traditional, while custard, chocolate, cheese, and other fillings are also common. It is sold warm at festivals, shopping streets, and specialty stalls, with the crispness of the shell varying by shop.

name: Dango
description: Dango is a chewy Japanese dumpling made from rice flour, shaped into small rounds, boiled or steamed, and often threaded onto a skewer. It may be plain, sweetened, or coated with a sauce or bean paste. Dango is enjoyed with tea and appears at seasonal celebrations, temple fairs, and traditional sweet shops.

name: Kakigori
description: Kakigori is a Japanese dessert of finely shaved ice flavored with fruit syrup, matcha, milk, or other toppings. The ice is piled high so it melts softly in the mouth, and sweet beans, condensed milk, or fruit may be added. It is especially associated with summer festivals, cafés, and shaved-ice shops.

name: Mochi
description: Mochi is a soft, elastic cake made from pounded or steamed glutinous rice. It can be grilled, added to soups, or served with sweet bean paste, soybean flour, or other fillings. Mochi appears in everyday sweets and important seasonal foods, especially around New Year, when careful eating is customary because of its chewiness.

name: Daifuku
description: Daifuku is a round mochi confection wrapped around a sweet filling, most traditionally smooth or chunky red bean paste. Modern versions may include whipped cream, fruit, custard, or ice cream. The soft rice-cake exterior and compact filling make it a common gift, tea sweet, and convenience-store dessert.

name: Warabi mochi
description: Warabi mochi is a translucent, softly chewy Japanese confection traditionally made with bracken starch or a similar starch. Pieces are usually chilled, cut into bite-sized shapes, and coated with roasted soybean flour, with brown sugar syrup sometimes added. It is a summer sweet sold by wagashi shops, cafés, and festival vendors.

name: Dorayaki
description: Dorayaki is a Japanese sweet made from two round, soft castella-like pancakes joined by a layer of sweet red bean paste. Some versions include chestnut, custard, or whipped cream. It is commonly served with tea, sold in confectionery shops and convenience stores, and packed individually as an easy snack or gift.

name: Castella
description: Castella is a moist Japanese sponge cake made with flour, eggs, sugar, and syrup, traditionally baked into a rectangular loaf with a smooth golden top. Its fine, springy crumb keeps well when wrapped, making it popular as a souvenir and gift. Nagasaki is especially associated with well-known castella shops.

name: Anmitsu
description: Anmitsu is a Japanese dessert arranged with cubes of agar jelly, sweet red bean paste, fruit, and small rice-flour dumplings. It is usually served with dark brown syrup poured over the components, and ice cream may be added for a richer version. The contrasting colors and textures make it a classic café sweet.

name: Melon pan
description: Melon pan is a sweet Japanese bun covered with a scored layer of cookie-like dough that becomes crisp during baking. Despite its name, it usually contains no melon; the pattern resembles the fruit's skin. It is sold in bakeries and convenience stores as a breakfast item, snack, or simple sweet bread.

name: Senbei
description: Senbei is a Japanese rice cracker made from cooked rice or rice flour, shaped and baked or grilled until crisp. Seasonings include soy sauce, salt, sugar, sesame, or seaweed, and regional recipes vary widely. Senbei is commonly served with tea, offered as a gift, or bought from specialty rice-cracker shops.

name: Yakiniku
description: Yakiniku is a Japanese meal in which bite-sized pieces of meat and vegetables are grilled at the table over gas, charcoal, or a built-in hot plate. Beef, pork, chicken, and offal are common, with dipping sauces served afterward. Diners cook their own portions, making it a popular social restaurant experience.

name: Nerikiri
description: Nerikiri is a refined Japanese sweet made from a smooth white bean paste combined with glutinous rice flour and shaped into seasonal flowers, leaves, or other motifs. Its colors and form often reflect the time of year. It is traditionally served with powdered green tea during tea gatherings and at wagashi shops.

name: Unagi kabayaki
description: Unagi kabayaki is a Japanese preparation of freshwater eel that is split, skewered, grilled, and repeatedly brushed with a sweet soy-based tare. The sauce caramelizes on the surface while the fish becomes tender, and the bones are removed during preparation. It is often served over rice and is especially popular in summer, though available year-round.

name: Ekiben
description: Ekiben is a boxed meal sold at or near a railway station for passengers to eat during a journey. Boxes usually combine rice with fish, meat, vegetables, pickles, and other side dishes, often highlighting local ingredients or specialties. Designs and contents vary by region, making the meal part of the travel experience.

name: Curry udon
description: Curry udon is a bowl of thick wheat noodles served in a Japanese curry-flavored broth, thickened so it clings to the noodles. Dashi, soy sauce, onions, and meat or fried tofu may be included. It is a warming lunch or dinner in noodle shops, and diners often use a spoon to manage the hot soup.

name: Yaki-udon
description: Yaki-udon is a stir-fried dish of thick udon noodles cooked with cabbage, onion, carrots, meat, seafood, or tofu. Soy sauce, oyster sauce, or another savory seasoning coats the noodles without a separate broth. It is easy to prepare at home and commonly appears at festivals, casual diners, and izakaya.

name: Sara udon
description: Sara udon is a Nagasaki specialty of noodles covered with a thick stir-fried topping of cabbage, bean sprouts, carrots, seafood, pork, and other ingredients. Despite the name, the noodles may be thin and crisp or thicker and soft depending on the style. It is served as a shared meal or substantial individual plate.

name: Tanmen
description: Tanmen is a Japanese noodle soup topped with a generous mound of stir-fried vegetables and usually pork. Cabbage, bean sprouts, carrots, onions, and mushrooms are common, while the broth is lightly seasoned rather than heavily rich. It is associated with casual Chinese-style restaurants and is often chosen as a balanced, filling meal.

name: Champon
description: Champon is a Nagasaki noodle dish in which seafood, pork, vegetables, and noodles cook together in a rich, milky broth. The noodles are added directly to the pot rather than boiled separately, allowing them to absorb the stock. It is a substantial one-bowl meal found in restaurants throughout Nagasaki and beyond.

name: Unadon
description: Unadon is a rice bowl topped with grilled freshwater eel brushed repeatedly with sweet soy-based tare. The eel is cooked until tender and smoky, while the sauce seasons the steamed rice beneath it. Restaurants may serve it in lacquered bowls, and it is a familiar celebratory meal as well as a summer favorite.

name: Tekkadon
description: Tekkadon is a Japanese rice bowl topped with slices of raw tuna sashimi, usually over vinegared sushi rice. Soy sauce, wasabi, shredded nori, and green onion may accompany it, while some versions add grated ginger or a raw egg yolk. It is a straightforward seafood meal served in sushi shops and markets.

name: Soboro-don
description: Soboro-don is a Japanese rice bowl arranged with finely crumbled seasoned meat, softly cooked egg, and sometimes green vegetables. Chicken is especially common, with each topping kept separate for a colorful appearance. The sweet-savory flavors and crumbly texture make it popular in home cooking, lunch boxes, and casual family restaurants.

name: Hayashi rice
description: Hayashi rice is a Japanese Western-style dish of thinly sliced beef and onions simmered in a glossy sauce based on demi-glace, tomato, and red wine or similar seasonings. The stew is spooned over steamed rice and may be served with pickles. It is a familiar café, family-restaurant, and home-cooked meal.

name: Uni gunkan
description: Uni gunkan is a piece of gunkan sushi in which a strip of nori holds vinegared rice and a topping of sea urchin roe. The roe has a soft texture and marine flavor, so it is eaten soon after serving. It is found at sushi counters and seafood restaurants, often as a premium seasonal choice.

name: Ikura gunkan
description: Ikura gunkan is a gunkan sushi piece topped with salmon roe held in place by a band of nori around vinegared rice. The translucent eggs are salty, lightly sweet, and pleasantly popping when bitten. It is commonly served at sushi restaurants and seafood markets, where the topping may be paired with cucumber or grated wasabi.

name: Anago nigiri
description: Anago nigiri is a piece of vinegared rice topped with cooked conger eel, usually brushed with a mild sweet sauce. The eel is simmered or steamed before serving, giving it a softer texture than many grilled fish toppings. It is a classic sushi choice for diners who prefer cooked seafood.

name: Hotate nigiri
description: Hotate nigiri is a sushi piece of vinegared rice topped with a slice of raw scallop, valued for its clean sweetness and tender texture. The scallop may be scored or garnished with wasabi, salt, or citrus. It is served at sushi counters and conveyor-belt restaurants, often as a mild introduction to raw seafood.

name: Hamachi sashimi
description: Hamachi sashimi is a Japanese seafood dish of raw yellowtail sliced into bite-sized pieces and served without rice. The fish has a mild flavor, soft texture, and moderate richness, and is commonly accompanied by soy sauce, wasabi, and shredded daikon. It is widely available at sushi restaurants, izakaya, seafood markets, and home celebrations.

name: Kani maki
description: Kani maki is a sushi roll containing crab meat, usually wrapped with vinegared rice and nori. Depending on the restaurant, the filling may be real crab or a seasoned imitation-crab preparation, often combined with cucumber or mayonnaise. It is an approachable roll served at sushi shops, bento counters, and supermarkets.

name: Korokke
description: Korokke is a Japanese croquette made from mashed potato, minced meat, seafood, or vegetables, shaped, breaded, and deep-fried. Potato and beef is a particularly common combination, while cream-based versions are also popular. Korokke is sold hot at butcher shops, supermarkets, bakeries, and convenience stores as an inexpensive snack or side dish.

name: Menchi-katsu
description: Menchi-katsu is a Japanese fried cutlet made from seasoned minced meat, usually beef, pork, or a mixture, shaped into a patty and coated with breadcrumbs. It is fried until the outside is crisp while the center stays moist. It is commonly eaten in diners, butcher shops, lunch boxes, and sandwiches.

name: Ebi fry
description: Ebi fry is a Japanese dish of peeled shrimp coated in flour, egg, and breadcrumbs before being deep-fried. The crisp prawns are commonly served with shredded cabbage, tartar sauce, lemon, rice, and miso soup. It is a standard item at family restaurants and洋食-style diners, and a familiar home-cooked treat.

name: Tebasaki
description: Tebasaki is a Nagoya-style chicken wing prepared without a heavy flour coating, fried until crisp, and seasoned with a sweet-savory sauce, pepper, sesame, or other spices. The wings are eaten by hand and pair naturally with beer. Specialized izakaya and casual restaurants often serve them in shared plates.

name: Tsukune
description: Tsukune is a Japanese chicken meatball shaped around a skewer and grilled, often with onion, ginger, or other seasonings mixed into the meat. It is brushed with sweet soy-based tare or served with egg yolk for dipping. Tsukune is a common yakitori choice at izakaya and festival food stalls.

name: Grilled squid
description: Grilled squid is a Japanese seafood dish of whole or sliced squid cooked over a grill until charred and tender, then seasoned with soy sauce, salt, or a sweet glaze. It may be served on a skewer or cut into strips for sharing. It is common at festivals, seaside markets, izakaya, and summer outdoor events.

name: Japanese potato salad
description: Japanese potato salad is a side dish made from partly mashed potatoes mixed with Japanese mayonnaise, cucumber, carrot, onion, and sometimes ham or boiled egg. Rice vinegar, salt, and pepper give it a gentle tang. It is a familiar side dish in home meals, bento boxes, convenience stores, and delicatessen counters.

name: Japanese omelette
description: Japanese omelette is a layered egg dish cooked in successive thin sheets and rolled into a neat rectangular log. Dashi, soy sauce, salt, or sugar season the eggs, producing styles that range from savory to gently sweet. It is served at breakfast, in bento, alongside sushi, and as a simple side dish.

name: Japanese pickled vegetables
description: Japanese pickled vegetables is a category of produce preserved with salt, vinegar, miso, rice bran, or sweetened seasonings. Daikon, cucumber, cabbage, turnip, and eggplant are common, with flavors ranging from crisp and sour to mellow and savory. Pickles are served in small portions beside rice, soup, grilled foods, and traditional set meals.

name: Mabo tofu
description: Mabo tofu is a Japanese adaptation of mapo tofu, combining soft tofu with seasoned minced pork or another meat in a savory sauce. Chili bean paste, soy sauce, ginger, garlic, and sometimes sansho provide warmth and fragrance. It is usually spooned over rice and served at Chinese-style restaurants or at home.

name: Imagawayaki
description: Imagawayaki is a round cake made by cooking batter in a metal mold and sandwiching a filling between two browned sides. Sweet red bean paste is traditional, while custard, cheese, chocolate, and seasonal flavors are also sold. It is eaten warm from street stalls, shopping arcades, festivals, and specialty confectionery shops.

name: Mitarashi dango
description: Mitarashi dango is a skewer of chewy rice-flour dumplings coated in a glossy sauce made from soy sauce, sugar, and starch. The glaze is sweet with a salty depth and clings to the lightly grilled or steamed dumplings. It is a familiar tea sweet sold at wagashi shops, supermarkets, and festivals.

name: Ningyoyaki
description: Ningyoyaki is a small sponge cake baked in molds shaped like dolls, animals, or local figures and usually filled with sweet red bean paste. The soft cake is easy to eat by hand and often sold warm. It is especially associated with Tokyo's Asakusa area, but similar molded sweets appear elsewhere.

name: Yakiimo
description: Yakiimo is a whole Japanese sweet potato roasted slowly, traditionally over hot stones or in a dedicated oven, until the skin darkens and the center becomes soft and naturally sweet. It is sold from seasonal shops, trucks, and supermarkets, especially in autumn and winter, and is eaten warm without elaborate toppings.

name: Yakisoba
description: Yakisoba is a Japanese stir-fried noodle dish made with wheat noodles, cabbage, carrots, pork, seafood, or other additions. A sweet-savory sauce coats the noodles, which are often topped with seaweed, pickled ginger, mayonnaise, or bonito flakes. It is common at festivals, school events, home tables, and casual food stalls.

name: Yokan
description: Yokan is a firm Japanese confection made by setting sweet red bean paste with agar and sugar. It is cut into neat slices or molded into decorative forms, with chestnut, green tea, or other flavors added to some varieties. Yokan keeps well and is commonly served with tea or presented as a gift.

name: Monaka
description: Monaka is a Japanese sweet made from two crisp, delicate wafer shells enclosing red bean paste. The filling may be smooth or chunky, and modern versions can include mochi, chestnut, or ice cream. Because the wafers lose their crispness over time, monaka is best eaten soon after opening, often with tea.

name: Japanese Mont Blanc
description: Japanese Mont Blanc is a Western-style cake or dessert topped with strands or swirls of sweet chestnut cream. A base of sponge cake, tart pastry, or meringue may support whipped cream and whole chestnuts. It is common in Japanese patisseries and cafés, where seasonal chestnut versions appear in autumn.

name: Japanese pudding
description: Japanese pudding is a softly set egg custard, usually chilled and unmolded over a layer of dark caramel sauce. It has a smooth, delicate texture and a gentle sweetness, sometimes with a firmer texture than Western flan. It is sold in cafés, convenience stores, supermarkets, and home kitchens as a familiar dessert.

name: Matcha ice cream
description: Matcha ice cream is a Japanese ice cream flavored with powdered green tea, combining dairy richness with matcha's grassy aroma and gentle bitterness. It may be served alone or with red bean paste, mochi, or syrup. The flavor is common in cafés, dessert shops, convenience stores, and seasonal sweets throughout Japan.

name: Tamago sando
description: Tamago sando is a Japanese sandwich made with soft white bread and a filling of chopped boiled eggs mixed with mayonnaise and seasonings. Some versions include a whole jammy egg in the center. The crusts are often removed, and the sandwich is a familiar convenience-store breakfast, lunch, picnic item, or café snack.

name: Yakisoba pan
description: Yakisoba pan is a soft bread roll split and filled with saucy yakisoba noodles, usually with pickled ginger or mayonnaise as a garnish. The combination turns a noodle dish into a portable sandwich. It is sold at bakeries, school cafeterias, convenience stores, and train kiosks as a quick lunch or snack.

name: Japanese cheesecake
description: Japanese cheesecake is a softly baked cake with a light, airy texture and a mild cream-cheese tang. The batter often includes whipped egg whites, which give the cake its gentle rise and characteristic wobble. It is sold by bakeries and cafés, served chilled or at room temperature, and often packed as a gift.

name: Famichiki
description: Famichiki is a seasoned, boneless fried chicken fillet sold hot at FamilyMart convenience stores in Japan. It has a crisp coating and a portable shape designed for eating by hand, often straight from its paper wrapper. The product is a familiar example of convenience-store fried food and an everyday quick snack.

name: Tea
description: Tea is a broad category of Japanese drinks made by steeping tea leaves or roasted grains in hot or cold water. Green tea, roasted teas, and grain infusions are served at home, restaurants, workplaces, and ceremonies. Preparation, temperature, and strength vary, so the word may refer to both everyday refreshment and formal hospitality.

name: Green Tea
description: Green Tea is a Japanese drink made by steeping processed tea leaves in hot water, producing a fresh, grassy flavor that may range from sweet to pleasantly bitter. Sencha is a common everyday style, while other grades suit different settings. It is served with meals, offered to guests, and enjoyed hot or iced.

name: Hojicha
description: Hojicha is a Japanese green tea made by roasting the leaves and stems, which creates a warm, nutty aroma and lowers the drink's bitterness and caffeine. It is usually brewed hot and served after meals, in cafés, or at home. Its gentle flavor also makes it a common tea for children and evening drinking.

name: Mugicha
description: Mugicha is a caffeine-free Japanese infusion made by steeping roasted barley in water. It has a toasted, slightly bitter flavor and is commonly prepared in large quantities, chilled, and kept in the refrigerator during summer. Restaurants and households serve it with meals, and bottled versions are widely available from vending machines and shops.

name: Pocari Sweat
description: Pocari Sweat is a lightly sweetened Japanese sports drink containing water, electrolytes, and a mild citrus-like flavor. It is designed to replace fluids and salts lost through sweating and is commonly consumed after exercise, during illness, or in hot weather. It is sold chilled in bottles and cans, often from vending machines.

name: Calpis
description: Calpis is a Japanese fermented milk-based soft drink with a sweet, gently tangy flavor and pale appearance. The concentrated version is mixed with water, cold milk, or soda, while ready-to-drink bottles are also common. It is served chilled at home and in cafés, and its mild taste is familiar from childhood refreshment.

name: Nama Beer
description: Nama Beer is a Japanese draft beer served fresh from a tap rather than from a sealed can or bottle. It is usually a pale lager poured into a chilled glass, with a foamy head and crisp carbonation. Nama beer is common at izakaya, restaurants, festivals, and beer gardens, where it accompanies shared food.

name: Japanese mixed drink
japaneseName: 日本のミックスドリンク
description: Japanese mixed drink is a broad category of beverages combining a base such as shōchū, whisky, beer-style mixer, or another spirit with soda, tea, fruit, or flavored syrup. Recipes vary by bar and region, and drinks may be served over ice or tall and sparkling. They are common at izakaya, restaurants, and casual gatherings.

name: Hoppy Set
description: Hoppy Set is a Japanese bar serving of Hoppy, a beer-style carbonated malt drink, alongside a glass of shōchū. The customer mixes the two to taste, usually over ice, creating a low-alcohol drink with a beer-like bitterness. It is especially associated with casual izakaya culture and older neighborhood drinking spots.

name: Lemon Sour
description: Lemon Sour is a Japanese mixed drink made from shōchū, sparkling water, and lemon juice or lemon flavoring, served cold over ice. Fresh lemon slices may be added, and sweetness varies between bars and canned versions. It is a common izakaya order, usually enjoyed with fried foods, grilled dishes, or salty snacks.

name: High Ball
description: High Ball is a Japanese whisky drink lengthened with chilled sparkling water and served over ice, often with a lemon peel or wedge. Its light, fizzy style makes it easy to pair with food. Highballs are especially common at izakaya, yakitori restaurants, and chain bars, where they may be poured quickly from taps.

name: Chūhai
description: Chūhai is a Japanese mixed or canned drink combining shōchū with carbonated water and fruit or other flavoring. Lemon, grapefruit, ume, and tea-based variations are common, with sweetness and alcohol strength clearly labeled on packaged versions. Chūhai is widely consumed at izakaya, home meals, parties, and convenience-store gatherings.

name: Sake
description: Sake is a Japanese brewed alcoholic drink made by fermenting rice with water, yeast, and koji mold. Styles range from dry and crisp to aromatic, sweet, or cloudy, and it may be served chilled, at room temperature, or warmed. Sake accompanies meals, ceremonies, celebrations, and everyday drinking at izakaya.

name: Junmai Sake
description: Junmai Sake is a style of Japanese sake brewed from rice, water, yeast, and koji without added distilled alcohol. Its flavor can be rich and savory or clean and dry depending on polishing and brewing choices. It is served chilled, at room temperature, or warm, and pairs naturally with many foods.

name: Ginjo Sake
description: Ginjo Sake is a fragrant style of Japanese sake made with specially polished rice and slow, low-temperature fermentation. It often has floral or fruit-like aromas and a clean finish, so it is commonly served chilled rather than hot. Ginjo is enjoyed at sake bars, restaurants, celebrations, and tastings focused on aroma.

name: Nigori Sake
description: Nigori Sake is a cloudy Japanese sake that is coarsely filtered, leaving fine rice particles suspended in the drink. It has a creamy appearance and may taste sweet, soft, or gently tart depending on the brewery. The bottle is often shaken carefully before serving and is usually enjoyed chilled with food or dessert.

name: Namazake
description: Namazake is a Japanese sake that has not undergone the usual pasteurization step, preserving a fresh, lively character. Because it remains more active and perishable than ordinary sake, it is kept refrigerated and consumed relatively soon after opening. It is usually served chilled and found at specialty retailers, breweries, restaurants, and seasonal tastings.

name: Shōchū
description: Shōchū is a distilled Japanese spirit made from ingredients such as barley, sweet potato, rice, buckwheat, or sugar cane. Its flavor depends strongly on the base and production region, and it may be served neat, over ice, with water, or mixed with soda or tea. It is common at izakaya and home meals.

name: Imo Shōchū
description: Imo Shōchū is a Japanese distilled spirit made from sweet potatoes and koji, often associated with Kyushu. It has a distinctive earthy, roasted aroma and a full flavor that softens when mixed with water. It is served neat, over ice, or diluted with hot or cold water at izakaya and regional drinking establishments.

name: Mugi Shōchū
description: Mugi Shōchū is a Japanese distilled spirit made from barley, producing a clean, mellow flavor with a light grain aroma. It is often approachable when served over ice or mixed with water, soda, or tea. Barley shōchū is widely available nationwide and is a common choice for highballs and relaxed izakaya drinking.

name: Awamori
description: Awamori is a distilled spirit from Okinawa made with long-grain indica rice and black koji. It is generally stronger and more aromatic than sake, and may be served neat, over ice, with water, or in a mixed drink. Aged bottles are traditionally kept in ceramic vessels and are valued for their rounded character.

name: Umeshu
description: Umeshu is a sweet Japanese fruit liqueur made by steeping firm ume fruit with alcohol and sugar until the drink becomes fragrant and rounded. It is commonly served over ice, mixed with soda, or diluted with water. Umeshu is enjoyed as an aperitif, after-dinner drink, or gentle option at izakaya and home gatherings.

name: Engawa nigiri
description: Engawa nigiri is a sushi piece of vinegared rice topped with the muscle along a flounder or halibut fin, known for its rich texture and fine fat. The topping is usually served raw and may be finished with salt, citrus, or a little wasabi. It is a distinctive sushi choice at counters and conveyor-belt restaurants.

name: Natto
description: Natto is a Japanese food of fermented soybeans with a strong aroma, sticky threads, and a savory umami flavor. It is usually stirred with soy sauce, mustard, and green onion, then spooned over hot rice, often at breakfast. The texture can be unfamiliar to newcomers, but natto is a supermarket food and staple in Japan.

name: Karubi
description: Karubi is a popular yakiniku order of richly marbled beef, generally taken from short-rib or related rib and belly cuts. Thin slices are grilled quickly at the table and eaten with dipping sauce, salt, or rice. Its juicy fat and strong flavor make it a familiar starting point, though the exact cut varies by restaurant.

name: Rōsu
description: Rōsu is a familiar yakiniku menu term for loin-style beef, although restaurants may use several different cuts under the name. It often offers a meatier, less fatty contrast to karubi, with premium versions showing more marbling. Slices are grilled briefly and served with tare, salt, wasabi, or steamed rice.

name: Harami
description: Harami is beef diaphragm meat served in yakiniku restaurants, valued for its deep flavor and loosely grained, tender texture. Although commonly grouped with offal on Japanese menus, it eats more like an ordinary steak cut. Pieces are grilled over high heat and commonly seasoned with a savory marinade, dipping sauce, or salt.

name: Misuji
description: Misuji is a beef cut from the shoulder-blade area, recognizable by the line of connective tissue running through its center. Well-marbled slices have a rich flavor and tender bite when prepared appropriately. It is often offered as a premium yakiniku selection, served in small portions with simple seasonings that highlight the meat.

name: Seseri
description: Seseri is chicken neck meat, removed from around the neck bones and valued for its juicy fat and pleasantly springy texture. The small strips are threaded onto skewers and grilled over charcoal for yakitori, though they can also be cooked loose at yakiniku restaurants. Salt, pepper, citrus, or a savory sauce commonly accompany it, and the chicken is cooked thoroughly before eating.

name: Ichibo
description: Ichibo is a beef rump-cap cut served at yakiniku restaurants, offering a balance of pronounced beef flavor and rich marbling. It is often sliced across the grain and grilled briefly, then paired with salt, wasabi, or dipping sauce. Restaurants commonly present it as a specialty cut alongside other individually named beef selections.

name: Tontoro
description: Tontoro is a fatty pork cut usually taken from around the neck and jowl, sliced into small pieces for grilling. It has a firm bite and generous fat that browns readily over heat. Common at yakiniku restaurants and izakaya, it is often seasoned with salt and served with lemon or green onion.

name: Mino
description: Mino is beef tripe from the first stomach, served in bite-sized pieces at yakiniku and grilled-offal restaurants. Its pale flesh has a firm, springy texture, and thicker portions are often scored to make them easier to chew. Salt or miso-based marinades provide seasoning before the pieces are grilled and eaten hot.

name: Shimachō
description: Shimachō is beef large intestine prepared for yakiniku, named for the striped appearance of its surface. The pieces combine a chewy outer layer with rich fat and are commonly coated in a miso or soy-based marinade. It is a classic grilled-offal order, cooked thoroughly and enjoyed with rice, vegetables, or drinks.

name: Maruchō
description: Maruchō is beef small intestine commonly prepared as short tubular pieces with the fat enclosed inside. Grilling browns the surface while the interior becomes rich and juicy, creating a contrast with the chewy casing. It is a popular choice at yakiniku and grilled-offal restaurants, usually seasoned with miso, soy-based sauce, or salt.

name: Miso soup
description: Miso soup is a Japanese soup made by dissolving fermented soybean paste into dashi, with additions such as tofu, wakame, green onion, or seasonal vegetables. Its flavor varies with the miso and stock used. Served alongside rice at breakfast, lunch, and dinner, it is a foundation of home cooking and restaurant set meals.

name: Oden
description: Oden is a Japanese simmered dish of ingredients such as daikon, boiled eggs, fish cakes, and konjac cooked slowly in a seasoned dashi broth. Diners choose individual pieces and may add mustard or regional sauces. It is especially associated with colder weather, appearing in home kitchens, specialty restaurants, izakaya, and some convenience stores.

name: Sashimi
description: Sashimi is a Japanese preparation of carefully sliced seafood served without sushi rice, usually raw but sometimes blanched or otherwise prepared. Tuna, sea bream, salmon, squid, and scallops are common choices. Soy sauce, wasabi, shredded daikon, and shiso accompany it at restaurants, izakaya, traditional meals, and home celebrations.

name: Inari sushi
description: Inari sushi is vinegared rice tucked into pockets of fried tofu that have been simmered in a sweet soy-based seasoning. Sesame, vegetables, or other ingredients may be mixed into the rice, and shapes vary by region. The portable pieces are familiar in bento boxes, picnics, supermarkets, and casual sushi assortments.

name: Temaki sushi
description: Temaki sushi is a hand-rolled sushi format, often shaped into a cone of nori around vinegared rice and fillings such as fish, cucumber, egg, or pickles. It is eaten by hand soon after rolling to keep the seaweed crisp. Temaki appears at sushi restaurants and informal home meals where diners assemble their own rolls.

name: Chawanmushi
description: Chawanmushi is a savory Japanese egg custard steamed gently in a small cup with dashi and seasonings. Chicken, shrimp, mushrooms, ginkgo nuts, or fish cake may be hidden beneath its smooth surface. Eaten with a spoon, it is commonly served as a delicate side dish in sushi restaurants, traditional meals, and home cooking.

name: Hiyayakko
description: Hiyayakko is a chilled tofu dish served with toppings such as grated ginger, green onion, bonito flakes, and soy sauce. Silken tofu is common, though firmer varieties are also used. With little preparation beyond cutting and garnishing, it is a familiar summer side dish in home meals and a simple order at izakaya.

name: Yudōfu
description: Yudōfu is a Japanese dish of tofu gently heated in water or a light kombu broth and lifted out to eat with dipping sauce and condiments. Ponzu, green onion, and grated ginger are common accompaniments. Strongly associated with Kyoto and temple-area restaurants, it is also a simple warming meal prepared at home.

name: Zaru soba
description: Zaru soba is a chilled soba preparation served drained on a bamboo tray or similar dish, often topped with shredded nori. Diners dip small bundles of noodles into a concentrated sauce with green onion and wasabi. It is popular in warm weather, and hot soba cooking water may be offered afterward to dilute the remaining sauce.

name: Sōmen
description: Sōmen is a very thin Japanese wheat noodle, commonly boiled briefly, rinsed, and served cold with a dipping sauce. Ginger, green onion, shiso, and other garnishes add flavor to the delicate strands. It is a familiar summer home meal, though the noodles can also be served warm in broth as nyūmen.

name: Tantanmen
description: Tantanmen is a Japanese adaptation of Sichuan dan dan noodles, commonly served in a broth flavored with sesame paste and chili oil. Seasoned minced pork and leafy greens are frequent toppings, while soup-free versions also exist. Its balance of nutty richness and heat makes it popular at ramen shops and Chinese-style restaurants.

name: Yaki onigiri
description: Yaki onigiri is a Japanese rice ball grilled or pan-toasted until its surface develops a browned crust. Soy sauce or miso is commonly brushed onto the outside, adding a savory aroma while the center stays soft. It is served at izakaya, barbecues, and home meals, sometimes with broth poured over it afterward.

name: Hitsumabushi
description: Hitsumabushi is a Nagoya specialty of finely sliced grilled eel served over rice, traditionally in a wooden container. Portions are eaten in stages: first plain, then with condiments, and then with dashi or tea poured over them. The changing flavors distinguish it from an ordinary eel rice bowl and make it a leisurely restaurant meal.

name: Jingisukan
description: Jingisukan is a Hokkaido-associated meal of lamb or mutton grilled with vegetables, often on a domed metal pan at the table. The meat may be marinated beforehand or dipped in sauce after cooking, while onions, cabbage, and bean sprouts cook alongside it. It is popular in beer halls, specialty restaurants, and outdoor gatherings.

name: Hambāgu
description: Hambāgu is a Japanese hamburger steak made from minced beef or a mixture of beef and pork, usually combined with onion, breadcrumbs, and egg. It is served without a bun, often with demi-glace sauce or grated daikon and ponzu. Rice and vegetables accompany it in home meals, family restaurants, and Western-style diners.

name: Shōgayaki
description: Shōgayaki is a Japanese dish usually made from sliced pork cooked in a ginger-forward sauce with soy sauce, sake, and a sweet seasoning. Onion may be added, and shredded cabbage is a common accompaniment. Served with rice and miso soup, it is a staple of home cooking, lunch counters, and set-meal restaurants.

name: Soup curry
description: Soup curry is a Sapporo-associated dish of thin, aromatic curry broth served with substantial vegetables and often a chicken leg or another protein. Rice usually comes separately, and diners combine spoonfuls with the soup as they eat. Specialty restaurants commonly offer choices of spice level, toppings, and broth style.

name: Okinawa soba
description: Okinawa soba is an Okinawan noodle soup made with thick wheat noodles rather than the buckwheat noodles suggested by its name. The broth commonly combines pork and bonito, with toppings such as pork belly, fish cake, and green onion. It is an everyday regional meal served in specialty shops, markets, and family restaurants.

name: Gōyā champurū
japaneseName: ゴーヤーチャンプルー
description: Gōyā champurū is an Okinawan stir-fry combining sliced bitter melon with firm tofu, egg, and often pork or canned luncheon meat. The vegetable's distinctive bitterness contrasts with the rich, savory ingredients. It is a representative Okinawan home dish, also widely served in regional restaurants and izakaya throughout Japan.

name: Zenzai
description: Zenzai is a Japanese sweet commonly served as a warm azuki-bean soup with mochi or small rice-flour dumplings. The beans provide a soft texture and earthy sweetness, sometimes balanced by salted accompaniments. Its meaning varies by region, with some versions served without much liquid, and it is found in traditional sweet shops and home kitchens.

name: Anpan
description: Anpan is a soft Japanese bread bun filled with sweet bean paste, usually made from red azuki beans. The filling may be smooth or chunky, and the top is sometimes decorated with sesame, poppy seeds, or a salted cherry blossom. It is a longstanding bakery staple eaten for breakfast, as a snack, or with tea.

name: Fruit sando
description: Fruit sando is a Japanese sandwich of soft white bread filled with whipped cream and fresh fruit such as strawberries, kiwi, or mandarin oranges. The crusts are usually removed, and careful slicing reveals a colorful cross-section. It is sold in fruit parlors, cafés, bakeries, and convenience stores as a sweet snack or light dessert.

name: Ramune
description: Ramune is a Japanese carbonated soft drink best known for its distinctive glass bottle sealed with a marble. Opening the bottle pushes the marble into the neck, where indentations help hold it while drinking. The classic flavor is lemon-lime-like, with many other varieties available, and it is strongly associated with summer festivals.

name: Matcha
description: Matcha is a finely ground Japanese green tea powder whisked directly into hot water rather than steeped and removed. Its flavor combines vegetal freshness, umami, and varying bitterness, with a smooth or lightly foamy texture depending on preparation. It is central to Japanese tea ceremony and also served in tea houses and cafés.
